h1: Torque Unit Converter: Nm, lb·ft, and kg·m
description: Free torque converter. Instantly convert Newton-meters (Nm), foot-pounds (lb-ft), and kilogram-meters (kg-m) with NIST-exact factors for any spec.
intro:
This torque converter instantly transforms values between the three most common torque units: **Newton-meters (Nm)**, **pound-feet (lb·ft)**, and **kilogram-meters (kg·m)**. Torque measures the rotational force applied around an axis — defined as Force × Moment Arm. Engine torque ratings, lug-nut tightening specs, brake caliper bolts, and industrial fastener tables all rely on precise unit conversions, and a single mismatched figure can mean a stripped thread, a failed head gasket, or a wheel that comes loose at highway speed.

The key conversion factors are exact and NIST-traceable: **1 Nm = 0.7375621 lb·ft = 0.1019716 kg·m**. They come from the SI definitions of the pound-force (1 lbf = 4.4482216 N), the international foot (1 ft = 0.3048 m), and the standard acceleration of gravity (g₀ = 9.80665 m/s²). The same constants are used by SAE, ISO, ASME, ASTM and ANSI publications, so converting through this tool gives results identical to the figures in any modern OEM service manual.

Use this calculator whenever you're reading a European car manual that lists torque in Nm but working with a US-calibrated torque wrench in lb·ft, or when interpreting older Japanese motorcycle service literature still printed in kg·m. It is equally useful for industrial maintenance, aerospace fastener checks, robotics motor sizing (where ISO 9283 quotes Nm but US gearmotor catalogs quote lb·ft), and even physics homework. Enter any value, pick the source unit, and you get the equivalent in the other two — fast, accurate, with no rounding shortcuts.

Keep in mind that **lb·ft (torque) is not the same as lb·in (pound-inches)** — they differ by a factor of 12. Always confirm the unit prefix on your service bulletin before tightening. And remember that kg·m here refers to kilogram-*force*·meter, not kilogram-mass — the conversion already bakes in g = 9.80665 m/s² so you can read straight off the result.
keyTakeaway: **1 Nm = 0.737562 lb·ft = 0.101972 kg·m** — e.g., a typical car engine producing 350 Nm equals 258.1 lb·ft or 35.7 kg·m.
useCases: Converting a European car's peak engine torque spec (e.g., 400 Nm = 295.0 lb·ft) to lb·ft for use with a US-calibrated torque wrench when re-torquing cylinder head bolts.
Verifying wheel lug-nut tightening specifications: a common spec of 100 lb·ft equals 135.6 Nm — critical to avoid over-tightening (snapped studs) or under-tightening (wheel separation at speed).
Translating Japanese motorcycle service manuals that list torque in kg·m (e.g., 3.5 kg·m = 34.32 Nm = 25.32 lb·ft for an axle nut) into Nm or lb·ft for use with non-metric tools.
Checking industrial machinery fastener specs published in kg·m against ANSI bolt-torque tables expressed in lb·ft to confirm equipment-installation compliance (e.g., 10 kg·m = 72.33 lb·ft).
Comparing diesel truck engine torque figures across brands — e.g., Cummins X15 at 1,850 lb·ft = 2,508 Nm vs. Mercedes-Benz OM471 at 2,400 Nm = 1,770 lb·ft — for fleet purchasing decisions.
Calculating the proper setting on a click-type torque wrench (which reads in lb·ft) to match a brake caliper bolt spec given in Nm — e.g., a 110 Nm caliper bolt = 81.13 lb·ft.
Sizing an electric servo motor for a robotic arm: a payload requiring 12 Nm of peak torque converts to 8.85 lb·ft, allowing direct comparison with NEMA-rated US gearmotor catalogs.
Setting a precision torque screwdriver on bicycle stem bolts: a typical 5 Nm spec equals 3.69 lb·ft or 0.51 kg·m, so the calibrated tool can be dialed in regardless of its unit scale.
explanation:
## How It's Calculated

Torque is defined as the cross product of force and lever arm length: **τ = F × r**. The unit conversions derive directly from the SI definitions of force and length.

```
# Exact NIST-traceable conversion factors

1 Nm  = 0.7375621 lb·ft   (exact: 1 / 1.3558179)
1 Nm  = 0.1019716 kg·m    (exact: 1 / 9.80665)

1 lb·ft = 1.3558179 Nm    (exact, from 1 lbf = 4.4482216 N, 1 ft = 0.3048 m)
1 lb·ft = 0.1382550 kg·m

1 kg·m  = 9.80665 Nm      (exact, from g = 9.80665 m/s²)
1 kg·m  = 7.2330139 lb·ft

# General conversion formulas
Result_lbft = Value_Nm  × 0.7375621
Result_Nm   = Value_lbft × 1.3558179
Result_kgm  = Value_Nm  × 0.1019716
Result_Nm   = Value_kgm  × 9.80665
Result_kgm  = Value_lbft × 0.1382550
Result_lbft = Value_kgm  × 7.2330139
```

> **Note on kg·m:** This unit uses kilogram-force (kgf), not kilogram-mass. The kilogram-force is defined as the force exerted by 1 kg of mass under standard gravity (g = 9.80665 m/s²), per NIST Special Publication 811.

---

---

## Typical Examples

### Example 1 — European Sedan Engine Spec
A BMW 3 Series turbocharged inline-6 is rated at **400 Nm** of peak torque in the service manual. A US technician needs this in lb·ft:

```
400 Nm × 0.7375621 = 295.0 lb·ft
400 Nm × 0.1019716 = 40.79 kg·m
```
The technician sets the torque wrench to **295 lb·ft**.

### Example 2 — Japanese Motorcycle Axle Nut
A Honda CBR service manual lists the rear axle nut torque as **8.8 kg·m**:

```
8.8 kg·m × 9.80665 = 86.30 Nm
8.8 kg·m × 7.2330  = 63.65 lb·ft
```
Using a lb·ft wrench, the technician torques to **63.65 lb·ft ≈ 64 lb·ft**.

### Example 3 — US Truck Lug Nut
A Ford F-150 specifies lug nuts at **150 lb·ft**:

```
150 lb·ft × 1.3558179 = 203.4 Nm
150 lb·ft × 0.1382550 = 20.74 kg·m
```
A mechanic with only a Nm-calibrated wrench sets it to **203 Nm**.

---

## Common Mistakes

1. **Confusing lb·ft with lb·in (pound-inches):** Pound-inches are 12× smaller than pound-feet. Torquing a spark plug to "25 lb·ft" when the spec is "25 lb·in" (= 2.08 lb·ft = 2.82 Nm) will strip threads instantly. Always check the unit prefix.

2. **Using mass-kg instead of force-kg (kgf):** The kg·m unit means kilogram-*force*·meter. Treating 1 kg·m as simply 1 kg × 1 m without applying g = 9.80665 m/s² gives a result ~2% off and is physically incorrect per NIST SP 811.

3. **Rounding too early:** Using 0.738 instead of 0.7375621 for Nm→lb·ft introduces a 0.034% error — negligible for most use cases, but on safety-critical bolts (e.g., brake calipers at 250 Nm), this could mean an error of 0.085 lb·ft. Always carry at least 4 significant figures.

4. **Applying torque without accounting for friction/angle:** A torque-to-yield (TTY) bolt spec often combines a torque value (e.g., 60 Nm) *plus* an angle (e.g., +90°). Converting only the Nm value without noting the angle method leads to undertorqued fasteners and potential head gasket failure.

5. **Ignoring temperature effects on torque wrenches:** NIST calibration standards indicate that torque wrenches can drift ±4% when used outside their calibrated temperature range. A wrench calibrated at 70°F used in a 20°F shop may under-torque by up to 4% even with a perfect unit conversion.

---

faq.q: What is the exact conversion factor between Nm and lb·ft?
faq.a: The exact factor is **1 lb·ft = 1.3558179 Nm**, derived from 1 lbf = 4.4482216 N (NIST-defined) and 1 ft = 0.3048 m (international foot, exact since 1959). Therefore 1 Nm = 0.7375621 lb·ft. This is the factor used in NIST Special Publication 811 and adopted by all major engineering standards bodies — SAE J1939 and J1349 (automotive), ISO 80000-4 (mechanical quantities), ASME B107.300 (torque tools), and DIN ISO 6789 (torque wrench calibration). The number is irrational beyond 7 decimal places, but truncation to 4-5 significant figures keeps practical fastener calculations well inside the ±4% tolerance of typical click-type torque wrenches.

faq.q: Why does kg·m use 9.80665 and not just 9.8 or 10?
faq.a: The value 9.80665 m/s² is the internationally defined **standard acceleration of gravity (g₀)**, established by the 3rd General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) in 1901 and reaffirmed by NIST in SP 811. It is a defined constant, not a measurement. Using 9.8 introduces a 0.068% error; using 10 introduces a 1.97% error — the latter is significant for precision fastener work where a wheel lug torqued to 100 lb·ft instead of 102 lb·ft (a 2% gap) puts you outside many OEM tolerance windows. Always use 9.80665 for NIST-traceable results, especially in aerospace and medical-device fastener documentation.

faq.q: Is lb·ft the same as ft·lb?
faq.a: Yes — **lb·ft and ft·lb refer to the same unit**: pound-force times feet, the work-equivalent of one pound of force applied at the end of a one-foot lever arm. The notation 'lb·ft' (force × distance) is technically preferred by SAE J1349 and ASME B107.300 to distinguish it from ft·lb used in energy (foot-pounds of work). In practice, both notations are interchangeable in torque contexts, and all major OEM service manuals — Ford, GM, Chrysler, Toyota, Honda, Volkswagen, BMW — treat them identically. Pay attention only when the spec sheet uses 'in·lb' or 'lb·in', which is 12× smaller and a much more common source of stripped-thread accidents.

faq.q: What are typical torque specs for common automotive fasteners?
faq.a: Typical ranges by fastener: spark plugs 10–30 Nm (7–22 lb·ft) depending on whether you have a flat-seat or taper-seat gasket; lug nuts 80–165 Nm (60–122 lb·ft) depending on vehicle and wheel-bolt diameter (M12 to M14); cylinder head bolts 50–200 Nm (37–148 lb·ft), often combined with a torque-to-yield angle step (+90° to +120°); oil drain plugs 20–40 Nm (15–30 lb·ft) for M12 to M14 plugs; brake caliper guide bolts 25–35 Nm (18–26 lb·ft); brake caliper bracket bolts 80–130 Nm (60–96 lb·ft). Always consult the vehicle-specific service manual — these vary significantly by fastener size (M6 to M16), material (steel vs. aluminum), and whether the bolt is reused or new.

faq.q: Why do US car specs use lb·ft while European specs use Nm?
faq.a: The US automotive industry historically used imperial units (lb·ft) based on the foot-pound-second (FPS) system, codified in SAE standards from the early 20th century. European manufacturers adopted SI (metric) units after the 1960 international adoption of SI by the General Conference on Weights and Measures, standardizing on Newton-meters across Volkswagen Group, Daimler, BMW, Stellantis Europe, Renault and Volvo. Japanese manufacturers (Toyota, Honda, Nissan, Mazda) often used kg·m historically — pre-1990 service manuals are full of them — but have largely transitioned to Nm in modern service manuals, reflecting global SI adoption. Some Korean and Chinese OEMs still publish dual-unit spec sheets to ease global service-network adoption.

faq.q: How accurate do I need to be when converting torque for fastener work?
faq.a: For general maintenance (oil changes, body panels, interior trim), rounding to the nearest whole number in lb·ft or Nm is sufficient — the bolts are forgiving and the tools are ±10% accurate. For **safety-critical fasteners** — lug nuts, brake calipers, suspension components, steering linkages, and cylinder heads — use at least 3 significant figures (e.g., 135.6 Nm, not 136 Nm) and use a calibrated wrench rated ±4% or better, per ASME B107.300. Over-torquing by 10–15% can permanently stretch or snap bolts (especially TTY bolts); under-torquing by the same margin risks loosening under vibration, which on a wheel can cause catastrophic separation at highway speed. When in doubt, follow the OEM spec exactly and use a torque-angle gauge for TTY procedures.

faq.q: Can I use this converter for industrial machinery and not just automotive use?
faq.a: Absolutely. The conversion factors (1 Nm = 0.7375621 lb·ft = 0.1019716 kg·m) are **universal physics constants** — they apply equally to industrial gearboxes, electric motor shaft torque ratings (NEMA MG 1 uses lb·ft; IEC 60034 uses Nm), CNC machine spindle ratings, robotics (Nm is the SI standard in ROS, ISO 9283 and ISO 10218), aerospace fastener specs (MIL-HDBK-60 mixes lb·in, lb·ft and Nm), pipeline flange bolting per ASME B16.5 (typically published in lb·ft), wind-turbine bolt assembly procedures (Nm with TTY angle), and oilfield well-head torquing (often lb·ft for legacy installations). The math is identical regardless of application — only the typical magnitudes differ. A wind-turbine main shaft bolt may need 4,000 Nm; an electronics screw may need 0.3 Nm.

faq.q: What's the difference between torque and work/energy if both can be measured in Nm?
faq.a: Torque (Nm) and energy/work (Joules, also Nm) are dimensionally identical but physically distinct. Torque is a vector — it describes rotational force at a point, not energy transferred. One Joule of work = force × displacement through space. One Nm of torque = force × lever arm, with no implied motion. The SAE and NIST both recommend using 'N·m' for torque and 'J' for energy to avoid confusion, even though the base units are the same. In OEM service manuals the convention is universally 'Nm' for torque values, never 'J'.

faq.q: How do I convert torque to horsepower at a given engine RPM?
faq.a: The standard formula in US units is **Power (hp) = Torque (lb·ft) × RPM ÷ 5252**. The constant 5252 comes from 33,000 ft·lb/min per hp divided by 2π. In metric units the relation is **Power (kW) = Torque (Nm) × RPM ÷ 9549**. For example, an engine producing 400 lb·ft at 4,000 RPM delivers 400 × 4000 ÷ 5252 = 305 hp. Note that peak torque and peak power normally occur at different RPMs, which is why dyno charts plot both curves separately. The two curves always intersect exactly at 5252 RPM when torque is expressed in lb·ft.

faq.q: Should I use a beam-type, click-type, or digital electronic torque wrench?
faq.a: Beam-type wrenches are cheap, robust, and accurate to about ±4%, but require you to read a scale while applying force — not ideal for tight engine bays. Click-type wrenches give an audible/tactile signal at the set value and are accurate to ±4% within their middle 80% of range, per ASME B107.300-2010; they need re-calibration every 5,000 cycles or annually. Digital electronic wrenches measure to ±2% across the full range and store readings, useful for audit trails on safety-critical work. For lug nuts and basic engine work a click-type is the industry standard; for cylinder-head TTY procedures and aerospace work, digital is preferred. Always set click-types back to their lowest value after use to relax the spring.

faq.q: What torque does a typical bicycle or e-bike fastener require, and why is it so low?
faq.a: Bicycle component specs range roughly 4–6 Nm (3–4.5 lb·ft) for stem and handlebar bolts, 5–7 Nm (3.7–5.2 lb·ft) for seatpost clamps, and 12–14 Nm (8.9–10.3 lb·ft) for crank arm bolts on modern alloy frames. Carbon fiber components are deliberately under-engineered in clamping force because exceeding the spec crushes the carbon weave irreversibly — manufacturers like Specialized and Trek explicitly publish 5 Nm limits and recommend a calibrated torque key (e.g., the Park Tool ATD-1) for every install. The low values are why a standard 1/2" drive wrench (typically calibrated 20–150 lb·ft) is too coarse — you need a 1/4" or smaller wrench rated for low-range work.
